IM11-01.note: GCF*LCM = product of the two numbers: 24n = 6*360 = 2160, n = 90; check gcf(24,90)=6 and lcm=360. Unique. Stem does not print the gcd*lcm identity, so the relation is genuinely tested. Ceiling on difficulty is that with four options a student can just test each: 15 fails divisibility by 6 at a glance, gcf(24,144)=24, gcf(24,60)=12. Back-solving is faster than the identity, which caps this at medium. 144 = 24*6 and 15 = 360/24 are real error endpoints; 60 = 360/6 is thinner.

IM11-02.note: Three-set inclusion-exclusion: 22+20+18 - (10+9+8) + 5 = 38, so 40-38 = 2. The pairwise counts read as inclusive of the triple overlap, which is the standard convention and the only one that yields an integer-consistent Venn diagram, so no ambiguity. 7 is exactly the omit-the-triple-add-back answer and 5 is the triple itself; both are endpoints of errors students actually make. Genuinely hard for ISEE Upper: three-set I-E with no diagram supplied.

IM11-03.note: Add the equations: 8x+8y = 72, so x+y = 9. 72 is the intermediate you compute on the way and 36 is the halve-instead-of-eighth slip; both are the right kind of trap rather than a leak, since neither is reachable by inspection. 5 is the weakest of the three.

IM11-04.note: 1#4 = 1 - 8 = -7; 3#(-7) = 9 + 14 = 23. Parenthesisation makes evaluation order unambiguous. 41 is the left-association error ((3#1)#4 = 7#4 = 41), -5 is the sign slip on -2b with b negative, 17 is a^2 + 2b. Every distractor is the endpoint of a named error.

IM11-05.note: Diagonal 10 gives side 10/sqrt2, area = d^2/2 = 50. No formula supplied, so the item tests the diagonal-side relation rather than substitution - the s10 defect is absent here. 100 (treating the diagonal as the side) is the dominant error and 200 is d^2*2; 48 corresponds to no error path I can name and is the filler of the set.

IM11-06.note: 16/144 = 11.11% -> 11.1. 33.3 (linear ratio 4/12 instead of area ratio) is the error this item exists to catch and it is strong. Partial reachability worth recording: 88.9 and 11.1 sum to 100, a constant the configuration supplies but the stem never prints, so a test-savvy student can see the complement pair and then pick the smaller because a 4-inch bull's-eye visibly covers well under half. That narrows four options to two without any area work. Not enough to call the key free, but it is the one sum-to-constant pair in the set.

IM11-07.note: (-3)^3 = -27, (-2)^4 = +16, sum -11. The four options are exactly the four sign combinations of 27 and 16, which is the ideal distractor set for a sign item. Easy on the real exam - one computation, no modelling.

IM11-08.note: 15 values, the 8th is the median; positions 1-5 are 0, 6-7 are 1, 8-10 are 2, so the median is 2. Counts sum to 15, consistent. 0 is the mode, 1 is an off-by-a-few miscount, 1.5 is the average-the-two-middles error transplanted to an odd-sized set. Easy: the only demand is reading a frequency list.

IM11-09.note: Common difference 3 with first term 5, so 3n+2 = 152. 150 (3*50, forgetting the constant) and 147 (3*49) are the two standard off-by-one failures and 149 is the third. Medium rather than easy because the whole item is the +2 offset.

IM11-10.note: Slope (2-8)/(5-2) = -2, y = -2x + 12, y = 0 at x = 6. Note that -2 is on the ballot and is the slope, i.e. an intermediate you compute on the way - here that is the intended trap (student reports the slope) rather than a leak, since it is not reachable by inspection. 3.5 is the midpoint x. 4 has no error path I can reconstruct.

IM11-11.note: Closing speed 28 mph, 84/28 = 3 hours. All three distractors are 84 divided by the wrong rate: 84/4 = 21 (difference of speeds), 84/12 = 7, 84/16 = 5.25. Clean set, but a one-step rate item on the real exam.

IM11-12.note: Marta is 30 in 8 years; 30 = 2(b+8) gives b+8 = 15, b = 7. 15 is the brother's age at the future time - the answer-the-wrong-question trap, and it is correctly on the ballot. 11 is 22/2 (applying the doubling now). Medium.

IM11-13.note: 6/3 = 2, 10^8/10^5 = 10^3, so 2000. 18000 is multiply-instead-of-divide the mantissas, 200 is an exponent off by one. 3000 corresponds to nothing I can name. Easy.

IM11-14.note: LEAK, the clearest one in the batch. 6x^3 = 48, x = 2 - but the item does not need to be solved. Three of the four options, 2, 4 and 6, are themselves in the ratio 1:2:3, so a student who reads only 'edges in the ratio 1:2:3' and 'shortest edge' can recognise the option set as the edge triple and take the smallest member; 8 is the only option outside it. The volume, the cube root and the factor of 6 are all bypassed. Exclusivity is intact - 2 is still the unique correct value - but the key is reachable without solving, and I have graded difficulty as the item actually plays rather than as the arithmetic suggests. Fix by replacing 4 and 6 with values off the 1:2:3 line (e.g. 3 for cube-root-of-48-ish slips, 8 stays as the x^3 intermediate).

IM11-15.note: r^2 = 162/18 = 9, r = 3. 9 is the r^2 intermediate, 54 is the arithmetic-mean-style slip, 4.5 is 9/2. Minor point against the protocol's inverse test: 'of positive numbers' exists to exclude r = -3, and -3 is NOT on the ballot, so that clause is decorative here - a student who solved to r = +/-3 and ignored the restriction still scores. It costs nothing to make -3 the fourth option and would make the clause load-bearing.

IM11-16.note: Sum is 50, median 12, so with a<=b<=c=12<=d<=e minimise a=b=1 and d=12, giving e = 50-26 = 24, and 24 >= 12 is consistent. Unique maximum. 26 is the answer you get by letting d drop below the median, 36 is 50-14 (forgetting the fourth element entirely), 12 is the median itself. Genuinely hard: a constructive optimisation under an order constraint, the only item here that would separate strong ISEE Upper candidates. One cosmetic point: 12 + 24 = 36 puts a sum relation among three of the four options, though it does not identify the key.

IM11-17.note: Vertices named in order, so AB is parallel to DC and D = A + C - B = (3, 6). The phrase 'in order' is doing real work and the option it exists to exclude, (11, 6) = B + C - A, is on the ballot - this is the inverse test passing. The four options are the full cross product of {3,11} x {2,6}, which is neutral: no option is the sum or difference of the others in a way that points anywhere.

IM11-18.note: 18, 27, 36, 45, 54, 63, 72, 81, 90 - nine of them; 09 is not a two-digit number and 99 sums to 18. 8 is the forget-90 count and 10 is the count-09 error, both real. 4 corresponds to nothing. Worth flagging that the key, 9, is numerically identical to the digit sum the stem prints; that usually pushes a savvy guesser away from it rather than toward it, so it is not a leak, but it is the one item where an option equals a stated quantity.

IM11-19.note: 350/28 = 12.5 gallons at $3.60 = $45.00. $12.50 is the gallons intermediate wearing a dollar sign, $100.80 is 28*3.60 (dividing by the wrong quantity), $46.80 is 13*3.60 (rounding 12.5 up). All three are errors students make. Easy.

IM11-20.note: 40*14 = 560; 686-560 = 126; 126/21 = 6 overtime hours. The stem asks for overtime hours and 46 (total hours worked) is on the ballot, which is the right construction. Small structural note: the options form two pairs 40 apart (46/6 and 49/9), so a student who notices the pairing knows the answer is one of the two small values, but still has to do the pay arithmetic to choose between them.

IM11-21.note: Multiples of 4 strictly between 50 and 150 run 52 to 148, 25 terms, sum 25*(52+148)/2 = 2500. 'Between' is exclusive but 150 is not a multiple of 4 anyway, so the boundary reading cannot change the answer - no ambiguity. 2448 drops the 52 term, 2652 adds a 152 term, 2400 is 24 terms. Medium, not hard: once you know the series formula the rest is arithmetic, which is knowledge-gating rather than reasoning.

IM11-22.note: -4 - 15 = -19. 6 p.m. to 11 p.m. is exactly the five hours the stem states, so the count is not a trap. -15 ignores the starting temperature, -22 uses six hours, 11 is the magnitudes added without signs. Easy.

IM11-23.note: 3.0472: tenths 0, hundredths 4, thousandths 7. The three distractors are the adjacent place values in both directions, which is the correct set for a place-value item. Easy - pure recall, and the easiest item in the batch.

IM11-24.note: 18 won, 12 lost, 18:12 = 3:2. 2 to 3 is the reversal, 3 to 5 is won-to-total, 5 to 3 is total-to-won reversed. Note the options are two reciprocal pairs, so a student who only reasons 'more wins than losses, ratio must exceed 1' halves the field to {5 to 3, 3 to 2} - but that is elimination a correct solver would do anyway, and the remaining choice needs the real reduction.

IM11-25.note: 2 1/3 = 7/3 = 14/6, so 14 sixths. 42 is 7*6 (multiplying by the denominator without reducing the thirds), 7 is the numerator of 7/3, 12 is 2*6 (dropping the fraction). Easy.

IM11-26.note: Area = base * height = 10 * 6 = 60; the 8-cm side is the red herring the item is built around. No formula is printed, so this is the s10 fix working as intended - the item tests whether the student knows the height is not the slant side. 80 = 10*8 is the dominant error, 48 = 8*6, 30 halves it as if it were a triangle. Strong set.

IM11-27.note: (2/5)^2 = 4/25. The clause 'the spins do not affect each other' is load-bearing and the option it excludes is on the ballot: 1/10 = (2/5)(1/4) is the without-replacement reading. 2/5 is the single-spin probability and 4/5 is the doubled one. This is the inverse test passing cleanly - the best-constructed option set in the batch.

IM11-28.note: 1.2n = n + 6, so 0.2n = 6 and n = 30. 36 is the increased result (an intermediate, correctly trapped), 5 is 6/1.2, 120 comes from treating 6 as the 5 percent. Medium at most - one equation.

IM11-29.note: The middle of five consecutive integers is S/5, so the least is S/5 - 2. S/5 + 2 is the greatest, S/5 is the middle, (S-2)/5 is the mis-placed subtraction. All three name a real confusion. Medium: symbolic rather than numeric, which is the harder register for this population, but the structure is standard.

IM11-30.note: 5:3 of 32 is 20 boys and 12 girls; 20/4 = 5 and 12/3 = 4, total 9. Four steps, all elementary. 5 is the boys-only intermediate, 23 is 32-9, 8 is 32/4. 8 is the weakest of the three. Medium on length, not on any single step.
